title: INSTALLING AND UPDATING SOFTWARE PACKAGES
display: Ch 14 — INSTALLING AND UPDATING SOFTWARE PACKAGES

content.text: Book reference: Chapter 14, pages 475–526. Guided Exercises: Registering Systems for Red Hat Support, Explaining and Investigating RPM Software Packages, Installing and Updating Software Packages with Yum, Enabling Yum Software Repositories, Managing Package Module Streams. Lab: Installing and Updating Software Packages.
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — This whole chapter
Package search/install/remove, repository management, and module streams are all standard, hands-on RHCSA tasks — and you already rehearsed the registration half of this chapter back in Part 0.
NOTE — yum vs. dnf — same thing, this guide uses dnf

This book (written for RHEL 8.0) uses the yum command throughout. In RHEL 8, yum is actually a symlink to dnf, the real, current package manager — every command below works identically whether you type yum or dnf. This guide uses dnf since that's the name you'll see in current documentation and man pages, but don't be thrown if you see yum used interchangeably elsewhere, including in your own command history.

sections.title: 14.1 Red Hat Subscription Management — a recap

content.text: You already did this in Part 0's setup, and it's worth recognizing that you were rehearsing real exam material: register (associate a system with a Red Hat account), subscribe/attach (entitle it to updates for specific products), enable repositories, and review entitlements.
Register this system to a Red Hat account
Auto-attach the best-matching available subscription (not needed on Simple Content Access accounts)
Show subscriptions currently attached to this system
Detach this system from the account entirely
Entitlement certificates live under /etc/pki/: product/ (what's installed), consumer/ (which account this system belongs to), entitlement/ (which subscriptions are attached).

Activation keys let a system register with a predefined subscription without a username/password — the standard method for unattended, automated deployments — but configuring them isn't covered at this course's depth.

sections.title: 14.2 RPM — the package format underneath it all

content.text: RPM (RPM Package Manager) packages files together with metadata (name, version, dependencies, license, changelog) and install/removal scripts, tracked in a local database so the system always knows exactly what's installed and what any given file belongs to.
The upstream software's own version number (2.4.37)
The PACKAGER's release number for that version — may not be the original developer (7.el8)
Target CPU architecture (x86_64, aarch64...), or noarch if the contents aren't architecture-specific

Only the name is required to install from a repository — dnf automatically picks the highest version, and within that, the highest release. Packages are GPG-signed, and RPM refuses to install anything whose signature doesn't verify against an imported, trusted key.
💡 Why this matters — Why the kernel package is special

Because a new kernel can only truly be tested by actually booting into it, kernel packages are deliberately built so multiple versions can be installed simultaneously — an update installs a new kernel alongside the old one rather than replacing it, so if the new one fails to boot, the previous kernel is still selectable from the boot menu.
Querying with rpm — for LOCAL package files/database, not repositories
Full detail (summary, license, size, install date...)
Which INSTALLED package owns a given file
The pre/post-install and pre/post-uninstall scripts a package runs
Same queries, but against a downloaded .rpm FILE that isn't installed yet (add -p)
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — rpm -qf is the classic "what package owns this file" tool

A frequent real troubleshooting pattern: you find a file and need to know what installed it (and therefore what to reinstall, or where to report a bug) — rpm -qf /path/to/file answers that instantly from the local database, no network needed.
rpm -ivh package.rpm # install a downloaded package file directly (-i install, -v verbose, -h hash progress marks)
⚠ WARNING — A third-party RPM can run arbitrary root-level scripts

Installing a package runs its pre/post-install scripts AS ROOT — this isn't unique to shady sources, but it's exactly why package provenance and GPG verification matter for anything not from Red Hat's own repositories.

You can extract a package's files WITHOUT installing it: rpm2cpio package.rpm | cpio -id unpacks everything into the current directory — useful for inspecting contents safely before committing to a real install.

sections.title: 14.3 dnf (yum) — the tool you'll actually use daily

content.text: Unlike plain rpm, dnf understands repositories and resolves dependencies automatically across all of them — this is the tool for anything beyond installing one single local file.
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — The core dnf command set — know every row
Every one of these is directly exam-relevant, and used constantly in real administration.
Find what package provides a file/path
Update one package, or dnf update alone for everything
Remove a package (+ anything that depends on it)
⚠ WARNING — dnf remove cascades — read the removal list before confirming

Removing a package also removes anything that DEPENDS on it (and anything depending on those, recursively). This can silently take out far more than you intended — always actually read the "Removing:" list dnf shows before typing y.

dnf provides is invaluable when you know a needed file path but not which package supplies it (e.g. dnf provides /usr/bin/ssh), the repository-search equivalent of rpm -qf for something not yet installed.
All install/remove/update transactions are logged to /var/log/dnf.rpm.log automatically, in addition to the interactive dnf history view.
Checking what kernel is actually running
dnf list kernel # shows every installed AND available kernel version
uname -r # just the currently RUNNING kernel's version/release
uname -a # full kernel + hostname + build details
dnf repolist all shows every configured repository and whether it's enabled. Repository definitions live as *.repo files under /etc/yum.repos.d/.
Create a new .repo file pointing at URL
Enable a repo for ONE command only, without persisting the change
⚠ WARNING — Never disable GPG checking on anything but a fully-trusted internal source

gpgcheck=0 (or dnf's --nogpgcheck) skips signature verification entirely — appropriate for a controlled internal lab repository you built yourself, and a real security risk anywhere packages could plausibly be tampered with or spoofed. The proper alternative is importing the source's real GPG key (rpm --import URL) and leaving gpgcheck=1.
🎯 RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — The content.example.com substitution from Part 0, revisited

The book's own guided exercise for this section has you point dnf at a classroom-only server — content.example.com — to install a placeholder package called rht-system, purely to practice the enable/disable-repo and install/update workflow. Your lab doesn't have that server, and doesn't need it: practice the exact same commands (config-manager --add-repo, --enable, --disable, install, update) against any small real package from your actual AppStream repository instead (e.g. cowsay or tree). The commands, syntax, and concepts you're rehearsing are identical either way — only the specific package name differs.

RHEL 8 splits content into two repositories: BaseOS (core OS packages, long life cycle, matches earlier RHEL behavior) and AppStream (applications, with modules allowing multiple versions of the same software to be available side by side).
A set of RPM packages that belong together, usually built around one application or language runtime (e.g. "postgresql")
One version-line within a module (e.g. postgresql:12 vs. postgresql:13) — only ONE stream per module can be enabled at a time
A named subset of packages within a stream for a particular use case (server, client, minimal, development...) — installing a module without specifying one uses its default profile
Every available module and its streams
Streams/profiles for one module, with [d]efault/[e]nabled/[x]disabled/[i]nstalled flags
Full detail on the default (or a specified) stream
Install the default stream's default profile (auto-enables the stream if needed)
Install a specific stream and profile
Remove the installed profile's packages (the stream itself stays enabled)
dnf install @modulename is exactly equivalent to dnf module install modulename — the @ tells dnf you mean a module, not a plain package.
⚠ WARNING — Switching streams is not a routine operation — it's a real upgrade/downgrade

Only one stream per module can be enabled; enabling a different one disables the current stream but does NOT automatically upgrade or remove the packages you already have installed from it — that's a separate, manual step (dnf distro-sync to reconcile versions, dnf remove for anything left over). Directly installing a different stream while the old one's packages are still present risks broken dependencies or data loss from upgrade scripts running against the wrong assumptions. Remove the old stream's packages FIRST for a clean switch.

sections.title: Hands-on: practice these on your own lab

content.text: 1. dnf repolist all on servera — confirm your BaseOS and AppStream repos show enabled from Part 0's registration.
2. dnf search all "text editor" — browse a few results, then dnf info on one that looks interesting.
3. sudo dnf install cowsay (or any small real package) — read the dependency/size summary before confirming.
4. rpm -q cowsay; rpm -ql cowsay — confirm it's installed and see exactly what files it placed on disk.
5. sudo dnf remove cowsay — read the removal list carefully before confirming, even though it's a trivial package this time.
6. dnf history — find the install/remove transactions you just made, then sudo dnf history undo <ID> to reverse one and confirm the effect.
7. dnf module list | head -30 — browse available modules; dnf module list nodejs (or another module present on your system) to see its streams and flags.
1. Q1 — You need to find out which installed package provides /etc/ssh/sshd_config. Which single command answers this, without touching the network?
2. Q2 — You run dnf remove openssl and it lists a dozen unrelated-looking packages to also be removed. What's actually happening, and what should you do before confirming?
3. Q3 — You want to move a module from stream 12 to stream 13. What's the recommended sequence, and why not just install the new stream directly?
Q1 — rpm -qf /etc/ssh/sshd_config — queries the local RPM database directly, no repository or network access needed.

Q2 — dnf remove cascades: it also removes every package that DEPENDS on openssl, and anything depending on those, recursively — a widely-depended-on package can pull in a surprisingly long list. Read the full "Removing:" list before confirming, since this can remove far more than intended.

Q3 — Remove the packages installed from the current stream first, then enable/install the new stream, using dnf distro-sync afterward to reconcile any remaining version mismatches. Installing the new stream directly while the old one's packages remain risks broken dependencies or data loss, since upgrade scripts may run against incorrect assumptions about what's already present.
subscription-manager register/attach/list — Red Hat's entitlement system, already exercised during Part 0's lab setup.
RPM packages bundle files, metadata, and install/removal scripts; rpm -q* queries the LOCAL database or a downloaded file, with -qf ("what owns this file") a particularly high-value pattern.

dnf (yum's modern name, symlinked together in RHEL 8) handles repositories and dependency resolution: search/info/install/update/remove/history are the core commands, and dnf remove cascades to dependents — always read the removal list.
Repositories are .repo files in /etc/yum.repos.d/, managed with dnf config-manager --enable/--disable/--add-repo; never disable GPG checking outside a fully-trusted internal source.

Application Streams let multiple versions (streams) of a module coexist in one repository, but only one stream per module can be enabled at a time — switching streams cleanly means removing the old stream's packages first, not installing the new one on top.
